HEEWON STYLE — a KOREAN WEBTOON movie still PAINTED like a premium digital painting, the look of a dramatic manhwa cover. A 2:1 movie frame composed for a 2:1 letterbox crop (nothing important at the top or bottom edge). The shot the scene names (wide establishing, two-shot, close-up, over-the-shoulder) from a dramatic camera angle (low three-quarter, worm's-eye, high overhead or dutch), never a flat straight-on catalogue pose. Named characters' FACES are drawn exactly like the attached character sheet: the same confident ink linework drawn BOLD and THICK with real line weight — a heavy tapered black contour around the whole silhouette and the hair mass, medium lines for folds and features, fine lines only for lashes and loose strands and manhwa face design (eye shape, brows, nose, jaw, hairline and hair), recognisably those characters, in the clothes the scene gives them. EVERYTHING ELSE IS PAINTED: visible textured brushwork — loose digital-paint strokes and dry-brush, charcoal-like hatching that follow every fold of the silk and every plate of armour, the shadows built from layered strokes, the brightest ridges laid in with single confident strokes, a faint paper-and-canvas grain; at the edges of the garments the linework breaks into loose sketchy strokes. NOT flat cel-shading, NOT smooth airbrushed gradients, NOT a clean vector look, NOT photoreal, NOT 3D. Night, worm’s-eye up the cliff at the west gate of Bisa: Tang soldiers climb a steep rock path and ladders against the stone wall under torchlight; at the top, a young Tang officer in steel lamellar heaves himself over the parapet, sword in hand, face fierce and terrified, a Goguryeo defender swinging a spear at him against the night sky. Torches, sparks, falling stones, men falling from ladders; far below, the dark bay with the Tang fleet’s lanterns. PLACE (match the battle map): the end of the Liaodong cape in early summer — a steep dark ridge with grey cliffs on every side and a Goguryeo stone fortress wall along its crest, a narrow inlet under it, a wide grey bay opening south to the sea. The Tang fleet of five hundred hulls comes up from the south out of the sea haze; a handful of Goguryeo warships row out of the inlet to meet it. Alongside, the Tang deck stands two men higher than the Goguryeo deck. BANNERS BY SIDE: vermilion Tang banners fly ONLY on the dark Tang hulls; red three-legged-crow banners ONLY on the Goguryeo ships; Tang sails are plain deep red, no emblem; the Tang sun disc holds an abstract black smudge, never a readable character. Goguryeo men in steel lamellar with red shoulder-wings and pheasant-feather helm plumes; Tang men in steel lamellar with vermilion cloth and round chest discs. BATTLE ACTION FRAME in the same painted look, NOT a calm posed still: a real battle caught mid-moment, like a frame from a big-budget animated war film. The camera is INSIDE the fight — low over the water among the oars, on a heaving deck, or at a hard dutch angle — with a dark out-of-focus foreground shape close to the lens (a gunwale, an oar blade, a shield rim, a banner, a burning spar). LOTS OF FIRE: sails and decks burning in painted flame with heat shimmer, columns of black and orange smoke, sparks and embers driving across the frame, firelight on wet faces and steel. ARMIES: dozens to hundreds of soldiers in frame at true human size against the ships — packed along gunwales, climbing, falling, rowing, loosing arrows — the nearest fully drawn and acting, the far ones massed painted shapes in the smoke. MOTION: spray thrown off oars and bows, arrows streaking in long lines, cloth, hair and banners whipping, bodies mid-leap and mid-fall, motion blur on the fastest things. EMOTION: every near face acts — screaming orders, terror, rage, grief, gritted teeth, soot and spray on the skin. WATER is a real painted sea — heavy dark swells, foam, fire reflected in it — never Hokusai claw waves, never woodblock or scroll stylisation, never flat cartoon shapes, never toy boats. The same ships, banners and shoreline in every frame of this battle. REFERENCE SHEET. TOP ROW, left to right: costume chart (cut and shape only; ignore its labels, poses and faces), banner goguryeo (field colour and emblem for that side's war-banners). BOTTOM ROW: the only sword design. Kingdom banners: copy field colour and emblem from the attached flag_*.png ref onto period silk war-banners — tall poles behind each side, long streamers, small pennants on spear-tips and saddle-backs. Painted silk, wind-whipped, torn and smoke-stained in battle; never a flat modern flag graphic. Each side's banner colour is the clearest colour on its half of the frame, so the kingdom reads at a glance. Tang banners: vermilion silk with a yellow sun disc and a dark brush glyph inside it — painted as an illegible brush mark, never readable text. Attached flag /flag_tang.png. Goguryeo banners: red silk with the black three-legged crow inside a studded black sun-ring. Attached flag /flag_goguryeo.png. Any sword is the ancient straight Korean ring-pommel dao: a small iron ring pommel, a short wrapped grip, a thin metal band and NO hand guard, a perfectly straight blade — never a katana, never a tsuba. BACKGROUND AND LIGHT (painterly tenebrism): the background IS the place and the moment of the scene — open sky if they are in the sky, the hall if they are in a hall, the gate, the river, the snow — painted loosely in atmospheric brushwork (drifting smoke, cloud, haze, mist, falling snow, embers) in the scene's own colours, soft and out of focus, with a faint bokeh of small lights; it has colour, weather and depth — never a flat black void, never a detailed set; crowds and armies only as massed painted shapes dissolving into haze. ONE hard directional key light that belongs to the place (a brazier, a lamp, the sun through cloud, a torch, moonlight) rakes across the faces and clothes from the side or from below, modelling them in high contrast with deep painted shadows and a thin edge of the same light along the silhouette. Each character's colour lives in that light and in the atmosphere around them — never a glow aura or halo. Faces and bodies act the beat: real expressions, real weight, mid-motion. Faces from the sheet; new poses, never the sheet's stance. Each named person appears once, never cloned. Everyone wears period clothing of their own court (Korean, Tang, Yamato, Mohe furs), never European dress. No text, no speech bubbles, no panel borders, no watermark. NIGHT GROUND: the frame is built on BLACK — crushed ink-black night masses around the subject, the place pulled out of the dark only where the one key light (fire, lamp, torch, moon) falls, small warm bokeh in the black; the figure is the bright thing in a dark frame.
